interviewQuestions.question: Implement an accessible tab component. Walk me through what makes it actually accessible, not just functional.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd build it against the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide's tabs pattern rather than inventing my own interaction scheme, since screen reader users have muscle memory from every other conforming tab set they've used — a bespoke keyboard scheme actively works against that.

The markup: `role="tablist"` on the container, `role="tab"` on each trigger with `aria-selected` reflecting the active one, `role="tabpanel"` on each content area, and `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` linking each tab-panel pair in both directions so the relationship is explicit to assistive tech, not just inferable from position.

The part that's easy to get functionally correct but subtly wrong on keyboard behavior: I'd use **roving tabindex** — only the currently-selected tab has `tabindex="0"`, every other tab has `tabindex="-1"`, and arrow keys move real focus between tabs directly via `.focus()`, flipping the roving index as they go. Without this, every individual tab sits in the Tab-key sequence, so a keyboard user has to Tab through all of them one at a time just to reach the content below — a real behavioral regression from how tabs are expected to work, not a cosmetic issue.

I'd close by testing it against the APG's own live example with a screen reader running, comparing announcements directly rather than assuming my implementation matches just because the roles look right.

**Testing:** whether you know the roving-tabindex pattern specifically, since it's the detail most implementations that "basically work" still get wrong.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Applied

interviewQuestions.question: Why should a team default to the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide's interaction pattern instead of designing their own for a custom widget?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The core argument is about user expectations, not code quality — a screen reader user builds cross-site muscle memory from every combobox, every menu, every tab set that follows the established convention. A component built to the APG pattern is instantly usable to that muscle memory the moment it's encountered; a bespoke pattern, even one that's internally consistent and well-tested, forces every user to relearn interaction specifically for this one implementation, with no real upside to justify the divergence.

There's a second, more practical argument: the APG patterns have already been tested against real assistive technology combinations by the working group that writes the ARIA spec itself, closing edge cases an individual team is unlikely to have thought through — what happens on Escape when the list is already closed, whether Home/End should be supported, how the pattern behaves in right-to-left languages. Reinventing the pattern means re-discovering all of that from scratch, usually by shipping the gaps and fixing them one bug report at a time.

The one legitimate reason to diverge is a documented, specific interaction requirement the APG genuinely doesn't cover — and even then, I'd extend the closest matching pattern rather than starting from nothing, so the divergence is minimal and intentional rather than accidental.

**Testing:** whether you understand this as a user-expectations argument, not just a "following the rules" one.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: You're reviewing a teammate's PR for a custom combobox component. What specifically would you check beyond "does it have ARIA attributes"?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd check the interaction contract piece by piece, since ARIA attributes being present says nothing about whether the coordinated behavior across the combobox's several moving parts is actually correct.

First, does `aria-activedescendant` on the input update correctly on every arrow-key press, and does it always point at an id that currently exists in the listbox — a stale reference here is invisible visually but breaks the screen reader's ability to announce the highlighted option. Second, does real DOM focus stay on the text input the whole time, rather than jumping into the listbox on arrow-key press — moving focus there would silently break the ability to keep typing while browsing suggestions, which is the entire point of a combobox over a plain `<select>`. Third, does `aria-expanded` toggle correctly on every path that opens or closes the list — not just the obvious typing-triggers-open path, but also Escape, selecting an option, and clicking outside. Fourth, does Enter commit the currently active option and close the list, and does Escape close without committing — these are easy to accidentally swap or conflate during implementation.

I'd also actually run it with a screen reader before approving, not just read the diff — this class of bug is specifically the kind that looks completely fine in code review and only surfaces when you exercise the real interaction.

**Testing:** whether you can review ARIA-heavy code for behavioral correctness, not just presence of the right attribute names.
